utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. There is difficulty with the translation. Let me see. Yes, everything is all right in the English. Let us try the French. Right, we'll see how things go. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one brief point. The chart that I prepared regarding the rebuttal time taken in the Lasva Valley cases I have distributed for the Court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we see that. Thank you for your industry but it's a little premature. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you are -- you have a doctorate in aerospace from the University of Belgrade in 1967?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, your report dated May 29th of this year has already been filed with the Court and it -- unless the Court wishes, you've already set forth your academic credentials and academic background. There appears to be no point to go through it unless the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, there's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the course of your extensive academic career and military career, Dr. Jankovic, have you had occasion to familiarise yourself with the full range of artillery weapons used in the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Among the calibres of weapons with which you are familiar, are you familiar with the characteristics, flight characteristics and fusing characteristics of projectiles used in 122-millimetre, 130-millimetre, and 152-millimetre calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that your first languages, if I may say, are French and Croatian; you are fluent in both?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you are fluent in written English and can speak the language but would prefer to testify in one of your two native languages?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who prepared the report to which I have just referred, the one dated May 29th of this year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I wrote the first draft part in Croatian and part in English. Then I was given the translation and the amended text was then delivered to me, and then I went through it once again amending it because, of course, there are technical terms and they need to be translated correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you receive any input or suggestions regarding the factual basis of this report or the expert opinions which you have rendered from us, the people who represent Mr. Kordic in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the other way around. The technical part is all mine. The only instructions I received concerned the format in which they should be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, sir, you have, I believe, read the testimony of Mr. Hamill who is in court today, I notice, the expert witness used by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read several things by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the opinions that Mr. Hamill rendered was based upon the fragments of two RGM-2 shell fuses handed to him by representatives of the intelligence services in the armed forces based in Zenica. Based upon the identification of those two fuse fragments as fragments from RGM-2 type fragments, Mr. Hamill opines that the calibre of weapon used during the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April 1993 was 122-millimetre. Would you provide the Trial Chamber with your assessment of the validity of that conclusion, Dr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That fuse, RGM-2 is used for three calibres, 122, 130, and 152. I have here the firing tables for these weapons and I can show them to you. Therefore, if that fuse was found, any of these three calibres could be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The RGM-2 fuse is also manufactured under licence, I believe, in the former Yugoslavia and bears the designation UTIU M-72; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not a licence. UTIU was designed in Yugoslavia but it was modelled on RGM-2. On the outside, yes, they are quite identical and they are interchangeable. I can show you the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually I have a picture here and I'd like to have it marked as a Defence exhibit, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D280/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, we've had put on the electronic monitor a photograph of these two fuses that I have just mentioned: the RGM-2 fuse, the UTIU M-72 fuse. Are these two fuses practically interchangeable in the calibres of weapon that you have mentioned or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, they are quite interchangeable. Their functions are exactly alike, and also as far as their dimensions are concerned, they are exactly alike, so that they are quite interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Based upon the presence of fragments of either one of these two fuses at a shelling site, sir, would it be possible to ascertain with any degree of scientific reliability the precise calibre of weapon used to fire the shell on which this fuse was located, or on which either of these two fuses were located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat: It could be any one of the three calibres: 122, 130, or 152. It is impossible to say a priori which calibre was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 10 of Dr. Jankovic's report, Your Honours, on page 5. Mr. Hamill also stated that some "very small pieces" of the shell were given to him, or the shells were given to him, for the purposes of trying to ascertain the calibre. And for the Court's reference, I'm referring to page 16.233 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it possible to ascertain the calibre of a particular shell, Dr. Jankovic, based solely upon visual inspection of very small pieces, such as those which were given to Mr. Hamill in 1997, I believe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, we establish if a piece belongs to a particular shell only if it is big enough, so that we can recognise it, recognise its geometrical shape. Small pieces are practically impossible to deal, all the more so since shells are made of special material which is special shell steel, so that -- and all are made of it so that not even the chemical analysis can be of any help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 12 of your report, Dr. Jankovic, you give some range data derived from the firing tables that are attached as four appendices to your expert report. There's only one question I would like to ask to you. You say that the maximum range or the normal range of a D-30J howitzer, the model which is of 122-millimetre calibre, is 15.3 kilometres. There's been some suggestion, and even some documents, I think, produced in this case that suggest that the range of that weapon is as high as 17.3 kilometres. Could you give the Court your views on the maximum range of that D-30J weapon and the basis for your views on that subject, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that the range of that weapon is 20 kilometres, because I personally designed a projectile in 1997 with a 20-kilometre range. It was presented in Abu Dhabi and it's well-known. So it simply depends. At the time that we are concerned with, that is under consideration by this august Court, such projectiles did not exist. We know that in Serbia, on the eve of the war, a projectile was designed and built with this range of 17.8 kilometres; however, I did not see that projectile. Croats, however, had two such specimens. One of them was taken a picture of so that it could be shown at the exhibition in Abu Dhabi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Other than these enhanced weapons -- actually, let me just ask you a background question. Is that an enhancement in the actual firing mechanism of the howitzer itself or is that extended range the result of an enhancement either in propellant or configuration of the projectile itself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is no kind of improvement of weapon, because the weapon is the same. The gun, the howitzer, is the same. There's nothing there. So the changes concern the projectile. There are different types of modifications: the base bleed, aerodynamic ones. We made the base bleed. The Serb side made aerodynamical constructions, and we did base bleed and the reconstruction of the projectile base in order to increase the -- to enlarge the chamber powder so as to increase the space available for powder. So if there is more powder and a better aerodynamical shape, that enables the Serb projectile to reach longer ranges. And we also redesigned the base, but that is not interesting because that was all in 1997, and I do not really want to tax your patience with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to 1993, Dr. Jankovic. Did these enhanced range projectiles exist for D-30J 122-millimetre-calibre weapons in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian side didn't have it. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. One minor detail. If I could ask the usher to put a previously marked Exhibit on the ELMO, D90/1, Your Honours, an ECMM daily report dated May 9th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, I believe that you have seen this European Community Monitor Mission report before. This is dated two or three weeks after the incident at issue and it concerns an investigation performed by the ECMM, specifically by Stavros Kinigopoulos and Major Lars Baggesen, into the firing point of artillery fire that fell on Zenica and Vitez on the 8th of May, 1993. Insofar as the Zenica shelling was concerned, the conclusion is that the artillery fire probably originated from a hilly area north of Travnik, an area controlled by the Bosnian Serb army. What conclusions can you reach from this report, sir, regarding whether or not Zenica was in range of artillery controlled by the Bosnian Serb artillery as of May 9th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did the measurements when I studied the material, and I believe that two weapons could have been used to shell Zenica: the one with 130 millimetres and one with 152. The 152 at the maximum range, and 130 has even a longer range. I believe the distance is something 24, because 130 has a 27-kilometre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you conclude from that, then, that the Bosnian Serb artillery actually had the range to hit Zenica, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is self-evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If I might turn to the last subject covered in your report, the crater analysis or so-called crater analysis performed by the European Community Monitor Mission. You have an extensive career Dr. Jankovic, both academically and practically. Have you ever seen any technical literature that deals with this so-called crater analysis, any academic treatises, any technical manuals on how to go about doing it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the sense that to envisage the crater of a particular calibre, yes, but not the other way around, that the crater can tell you what calibre was used. These are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, there have been a number of photographs that were used taken on April 19, 1993 and conclusions were drawn in various ways by various witnesses. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether, in your view, any useful or reliable scientific conclusions concerning the calibre of weapon, the range from which the projectile was fired, or the direction of fire can be drawn from photographs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tend to agree with what was said that it is evident that we are dealing with the contact action fuse, because it is evident that the explosion was not delayed so that is the first conclusion. Secondly, it is also evident that these medium calibres as we call them, so 122, 130, 152, and that can also be concluded it is also possible to approximately, but I repeat the word "approximately", one can approximately determine the direction from which the projectile came but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you tell the Court what are the major factors that affect ballistic trajectory of projectiles, unguided projectiles in flight?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The range, the range is initial velocity, muzzle velocity. So there is also one question when it comes to weaponry whether this initial velocity drops because of the fatigue or the age of the weapons and we had that problem in -- because if you have large guns which are very old, then there may be a significant decline in velocity. Then, of course, barrel elevation and so on and so forth. All that has to be calculated in case we're dealing with one weapon and in that case, the wind is very important because it can significantly affect the direction and the range, it plays the crucial role. It is then followed by air density, that is, the temperature and the pressure, the air pressure. Then the spin will also play a certain role and Mr. Hamill, I suppose, will understand this. In this war there was no normal logistics so the projectiles were all mixed up in terms of their weight. There were not classified gunmen -- practically should have their projectiles classified as to weight. However, in this war it was not the case. So that sometimes a projectile would fall several hundred metres short because in the same firing group -- because during the same turn of fire, people would use larger projectiles and smaller, the lighter and heavier projectiles. So these are all the things that have to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if we can break these variables down into three categories. I think that there is one that affects range, one that affects direction of incoming fire or -- and one that affects both. In terms of the effect upon range, ambient air temperature and ambient air pressure affect the actual distance over which a projectile can fly; is that fair to say? In terms of the drift or the direction of incoming fire, if you like, winds aloft are a critical consideration, are they not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it affects both the range and the direction because we have crosswind and a drift. But if we talk about a drift, one has to bear in mind that it is always the same. There is always declination towards the right whereas the other factors are scattered so to speak, unless they were being measured. And in the -- in this war, the Croatian army did not have the necessary equipment, instruments for that kind of measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The drift measurements that you identified were crosswind and gyroscopic precession causes a drift to the right as a result of the rotation of the shell?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a well-established fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence that any of the people who have testified regarding the Zenica shelling in this case considered any of these factors, sir? Let me just enumerate them: Winds aloft, ambient air temperature, barometric pressure, Coriolis force that results from the force of the earth, the gyroscopic precision effect as a result of the rotation of the shell in flight, tube life of guns used, the quality and consistency of the propellant, level of training of the actual people firing these weapons, and then the accuracy of the firing tables and maps available to the artillerymen. Were any of those factors considered in the conclusions reached and offered to this Court, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents which I reviewed, these data are mentioned and there were even some figures provided but some of them were quite mistaken. It was said, for instance, that if the artillerymen were well-trained, it would be about 50 metres off the mark. But if you do not take into account the wind, it can account for a couple of hundred metres. So it is very important to know what the logistics were. It was fairly primitive at the time, fairly poor, and not as it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see any others that Mr. Hamill or any of the other people who have reached conclusions regarding the direction of fire and the range and calibre considered the meteorological data, Dr. Jankovic, or any meteorological data to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see. I would only like to add that Colonel Lausten, I don't know exactly the name, he offered an opinion which would be close to reality as far as these ranges are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Based upon the materials that you have reviewed, do you -- can you state in your opinion, sir, whether it is possible or not to ascertain the calibre, the precise calibre of the shells used in the Zenica shelling on April 19th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely and categorically I concert that it is not possible to conclude which of the three calibres was used based on the fuse and based on the fragments found on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Based upon the fuse and based upon the fragment and based upon photographs of the crater, is it possible to determine the distance over which the projectiles were fired, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not possible, because if it was one type of projectile, then it would have been one distance, and even if we knew which projectile was used, I think it is absolutely impossible to ascertain, on the basis of the crater, the distance from which this projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Based upon those same factors, sir, fragments, fragments of fuses, and pictures of the crater, is it possible, in your opinion, to determine the precise direction of incoming fire, the firing location or the putative target?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The set direction is not possible to -- you can again determine a range. I tried to simulate the situation on the computer and tried to find out this range. If there was a strong crosswind, it would have highly affected the trajectory, and then that would not be the right direction. It would have been sort of the end direction. My calculation showed that I first took the 122-millimetre calibre because that is what was mostly considered. That first deviation is 1.5 degrees between -- for the drift, and the crosswind was -- is a very large factor. You can find that in the meteorological data so you can find those data for our own country for that time. So that would increase the angle to about 3.5 degrees, but it is very dangerous to calculate that simply while 1.5 degrees is a fixed component. The other one is more variable. So it is very hard to make a clear simple calculation of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Without having accurate meteorological data, can you make any conclusions about those three things that I enumerated; the direction of fire, firing location or the supposed target?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Without such data, it is impossible to give an accurate answer because for any simulated test, you need the accurate data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Jankovic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, I want to be sure that I have your evidence. The first matter is this: That you gave evidence about the range of the D-30J howitzer and you said that it was 20 kilometres. But that, as I understand it, was in 1997. You said that in Serbia, on the eve of the conflict, a projectile with a range of 17.8 kilometres was designed, but as I understood you to say the Croats didn't have one. So the question is this: What was the maximum range available to the Croats of this howitzer in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: 15.3 kilometres. I can add that the Croats used the Soviet projectile UF -- I think it's 486, right, and they had their own copy of that projectile. In other words, the same type of projectile was being manufactured in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the next matter is this, that you were referred to the ECMM report of the 9th of May which concluded that the projectile could have come from the area controlled by the Bosnian Serb army north of Travnik. And as I understood your evidence, you say that you, yourself, did the measurements, and you concluded that two weapons could have been used to shell Zenica, that is, the 130 and the 152. The 152 at maximum range and the 130, you said, had an even longer range. And then you said you believed the distance was 24 kilometres, and I didn't follow your evidence from then on. When you said you did the measurements, what measurements were you referring to in this connection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This was in the previous case. I was also called here to give my opinion in the case of Mr. Blaskic, and I studied the documents, and among the documents there were dispositions of the Serbian troops on Mount Vlasic which is due north of Travnik. I measured the distance on the map and concluded that it was possible to fire for Zenica from that location using these two weapons. That was on the basis of a statement by a witness whose name I cannot recall right now, but I can provide it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the distance to Mount Vlasic was 24 kilometres, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it was Mount Vlasic. Mount Vlasic is also due north of Travnik. But the location was pinpointed for me. I am not exactly sure whether it was on Mount Vlasic or not. I cannot confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But so we have the point, it was -- the area controlled by the Bosnian Serb army was 24 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the range of the 152 was 25, or is 25 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me to look. Twenty-four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, the scientific method, I think you can help us, the scientific method sometimes involves seeking a conclusion by one route and then seeing whether it's confirmed in a wholly independent way; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course wherever that happens, where conclusion 1 is confirmed by entirely independent conclusion 2, it's proper scientifically to add those two conclusions together and to strengthen your first conclusion; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move on? I don't know what to say to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't argue with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if we could put the front line map on the board, please. Make sure we've got the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's going on the board and just being straightened out, one other detail, Dr. Jankovic, please. I think in the Blaskic trial you gave a great deal of evidence about angle of elevation of firing and landing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It, of course, has absolutely nothing to do with the issue in hand, does it, and never did, for the various weapons and the various locations that may explain the Zenica shelling, where all possible, notwithstanding the intervening hills, because the intervening hills were so low; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it, as a matter of fact, your decision to give that evidence on angles of elevation and angles of landing of shells, or was it the decision of the lawyers in that case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The lawyer gave me documents. I read them. The documents of the Prosecution. And there were witnesses who spoke about those angles, and I then explained that the witness in that respect was not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you may not have seen this map, and it's always difficult to work with maps, even for people with your experience, so by all means, with the Court's leave, take as much time as you need to familiarise yourself with it. And I shall simply be asking you about the location of Zenica, the area known as Puticevo, and the Vlasic feature. So if you can just take your time, find those areas, and indeed, when you've found them, point them out to us, please. And there's a pointer on the desk if you want to use it. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, not to interrupt, but I wonder if we could have an identification of the exhibit number, because I can't see the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's 2612.2A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness has trouble finding the places, he should say so and then somebody can help.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness should also be given a microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know exactly where Puticevo is. I can't find it here. I know it should be somewhere here, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Due west of Zenica, and just before you come to the front line, red line marking, is the area of Puticevo. It's just off the road between Vitez and Travnik. Even if it's not marked there, that's where it is. I should have checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why don't you go and check now, Mr. Nice, and point it out to the witness, because otherwise we could spend some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is marked on this map. It's actually very difficult to read because of the enlargement of the map, but we've pointed it out to Dr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you've seen those three places, Dr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, are you happy with that, as happy as you can be with that plan? You can find your way around?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a similar map. Now I know where Puticevo is. That is one locality. I do not know what the other two localities are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vlasic you know. You've referred to Vlasic for us. Vlasic is, of course, in Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, again, I think, Mr. Nice, go and point it out. It would be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. That's all I want you to do standing up. If you'd be good enough perhaps to take your seat again, then we can press on. The position is actually quite straightforward, if not simple. Puticevo is pretty well due west of Zenica and is within Croat-held territory; Vlasic is pretty well north-west of Zenica and within Serb-held territory. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really say whether all that you are saying is correct or not. If I may, I'm a technical man and I'm a scientist. If these are facts, then they are facts. That is not the question that should be addressed to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to address them to you, but you've told us that you did calculations about the possibility of shells coming from Vlasic, and I assume that that included your being familiar with the maps of Vlasic. When you did your calculations about Vlasic, did you not look at a map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a map like this. It was clearer than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, please confirm: Vlasic is approximately --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And shall we now just deal with the last little bit of evidence that you were giving in answer to His Honour, the Presiding Judge, His Honour Judge May. The incident in the May shelling where you were saying, as the report suggests, that there could have been shelling coming from Mount Vlasic and from Serb-held territory related, of course, to a shelling in the month of May and did not relate to a shelling in the month of April; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The report which I wrote concerns April, and I did not say anything about Vlasic. In this report I only spoke about these things. And this report -- I did not comment on this in my report, on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, but you've been asked a question about it this morning, and I don't want there to be any confusion. So perhaps you'd take D90/1 at tab 11, which is what you were asked to look at, which is the daily report for the 9th of May. Now, you've got it in English, and we're fortunate that you read English. This document, the 9th of May, relates to yesterday, the 8th of May, Zenica being shelled. And then the conclusion is that the direction of shelling against Vitez and Zenica shows -- I hope I'm not going too fast, because it's not on the ELMO -- that the firing position was probably on the hilly area six kilometres north of Travnik -- [Microphone not activated] the Vlasic feature, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So whatever it may have to do with this case, it doesn't relate to the shelling on the 19th of April, does it? Can we now, please -- I don't know if you're going to answer that question, but can we now please go to your expert's statement, and it would help me if you'd have it before you. I have a few questions to ask on most pages, but only a few, because we're not in much disagreement, Dr. Jankovic, you'll be pleased to know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 1 -- sorry, page 2, as it is, but paragraphs 1 and 2 set out the history of your qualification, and very impressive they are, if I respectfully say so, but they're basically to do with aerodynamics of projectiles; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is distinct from working with shells and with artillery. Projectiles of this kind are different from artillery projectiles; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a ballistics expert; that is, aerodynamics is my basic field of research. But I was the ballistic expert in the military institute and I studied the projectiles, and I also told you that I designed artillery projectiles myself. I told you so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3, because we then move from what's set out on page 2 to what's set out on page 3. And then on line 2 you do say: "I worked from 1991 to 1995 at the Zagreb Maritime and Defence Institute on the problem of developing fire control and firing tables." Now, I don't want to take any time on this, but just explain to me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- was it a practical problem or a theoretical problem? Was it about new weapons? I don't know. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Fire control means developing software for gunmen which helps them to calculate various elements needed for targeting and firing, and firing tables, and I can show you the ones that I calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may not be necessary. By all means do, if you think it's important, but it may not be necessary. Then we come to the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are firing tables for Nora 152 with the Russian projectile, or OF 540.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter is sorry. Didn't get the second mark.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: But that was done after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see at the end of this paragraph, in the middle of the page, that your published articles and books include exterior ballistics, missile aerodynamics, and the mechanics of projectile flight. This would appear to be -- I don't say just theoretical, but it would appear to be perhaps theory, and high theory at that, and would appear to be concerned mostly with missiles. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I also dealt with guided missiles and at present I teach the flight mechanics of aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, thus far, unless I have missed it, you haven't identified any experience as an artillery officer, as a person regularly firing or supervising the firing of guns; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did really fire at the firing range, but not with units and I did not work with the army, with troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you haven't identified any experience then or since of the types spoken of by Mr. Hamill where post facto analysis of shelling is done by artillery officers. You haven't spoken of that type of experience.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have that sort of experience at all.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Except at a firing range when we engineers go to see the craters made by projectiles because that is rather important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on, just a couple of things, really. Are you aware that Mr. Hamill's work on that dreadful Markale market shelling was incorporated in an United Nations report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because I must suggest to you that it was, and that it included his analysis of direction built on crater analysis. Would you accept that that may have, indeed, happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as one of the witnesses who we've had reference to, a man, Baggesen, would you accept that when Vitez was shelled, along with Zenica, on the 8th of May, his conclusions were accepted by all sides based though they were, in part, on crater analysis. Would you accept that? It's in his war diary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have -- I do not object to any of these things, but I did not read these things and I cannot comment on them. I cannot say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move back to your report. I have no challenge to your paragraph three. And when you come to paragraph four, you say this, you have been asked by the Kordic Defence to provide an expert opinion regarding the shelling of Zenica on April 19th. It must have been a slip of the pen, but you can't provide any opinion on the shelling of Zenica itself, can you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We can always theoretically simulate events, that is how we analyse events, and that is what I understood was asked of me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may have not been clear but let me make myself clearer. You haven't examined the craters left by the shells yourself, have you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you do not offer an opinion one way or another as to where the shells that fell on Zenica may have come from.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that within a certain interval, one can accept that they may have come from, and I tried to measure that interval, and I said here that it was difficult and it was only with a certain -- that with a certain degree of probability, one could say what the interval was. For instance, for 122, I concluded that if these measurements were accurate, absolutely accurate, and then again probably an error is included there because there are errors in any kind of measurements, that that interval could be at least plus or minus five degrees. That was said roughly by Colonel Lausten or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to five degrees, and I'm only going to press you once more. What you've provided to the Court is some expert opinion on various topics including fuses, and your opinion on accuracies of certain types of measurements, but you do not provide on opinion on where Zenica was shelled from on the 19th of April because you don't have an opinion on that topic, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not give my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you don't have an opinion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand that. Either you do or you don't have an opinion on where it was shelled from.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again, if all those measurements were correct, according to the document that I write, I concluded that the most probable, the most likely but only the most likely was that it had come from the direction plus minus five degrees from the direction that was measured. So it could be plus five or minus five to the other side, so that was within that interval. That is my opinion. But it only applies to 122 millimetres and that is the most probable so it can be more, it can be less, but in all likelihood, that is five. I did not compute it for calibres because one would have to perform simulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have to deal with it later, we can deal with it straight away. Now, that we understand the map and, of course, look at it if you need to, but the Judges have seen it. If the calculation made by Mr. Hamill is honourably and properly made, to the effect came from due west and if you are allowing for a five degree maximum error or allowance, what is quite clear is that the shelling cannot have come from the Vlasic feature which is 45 degrees away; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not maximum error, but the most probable error at the maximum, that is the maximum can be infinite. But in practice, we take it for Gauss distribution that the maximum error is four times the most probable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But just so that I can understand that, and I was troubled by your narrative of the number of factors to be taken into account. If you multiply 5 by 4, that's 20. You are you really saying that firing of a major artillery piece involves a scatter of plus or minus 20, a total of 40 degrees of error? You can't seriously be saying that, can you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that is not what I said. I repeat, I know it is very difficult technical matters, so may I have some more time to explain it. We do not know what the wind was. In those areas of our country winds can be very strong at high altitudes even though there are none perhaps close to the ground. As these reports say that there was no wind, that the weather was nice, it does not mean that there was no wind up there, quite the reverse. It could have been very strong wind up there. And at these altitudes at which these projectiles fly, these are 5, 6, 7 kilometres or more, the wind there is 50, 60, 70 metres as a rule, 50 metres, but it can be faster or slower. And with these weather tables, I also have them with me, I can show you. Now if we have a wind of that order of magnitude, lateral wind, that angle can curve the path by 3.5 degrees. And then if you add that 1.5, that is five. But this wind can be even stronger and that was a very -- that is very likely. It could have been very strong, of course it needn't have been but it could have been very strong. So if it was twice as strong, then it will be a deviation of 7 degrees. If it was even stronger then the deviation would be even higher. So the 2.5 degrees are always the same, but the deviation caused by wind can be much more than that because of this high altitude wind, and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said something about maximum error being 4 times the most probable error. I hadn't understood how you could get 5 degrees from 3.5 and 1.5 and I must have made the -- an error somewhere in multiplying 5 by 4. What are saying, please, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- is the maximum error?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am talking about the most probable error, and the most probable error is about 3.5 degrees, and you said "maximum." If you want to talk about the maximum one, then we must multiply the most probable one by four times, that is, the Gauss distribution, that is the probability. And to this one, one has to add 1.5 because that is a constant value. It's always the time it doesn't scatter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, so that we are now up to a possible maximum error, 15.5 degrees, is that really what you're suggesting is the accuracy of these heavy artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, don't. The accuracy of artillery weapons is a completely different matter. The accuracy of artillery weapons is not what you are saying. All I said, because we do not know what the wind was. We need to assume -- we need to hypothesise a certain value of the wind and hence the error, because we are hypothesising the strength of the wind. And the maximum error which you calculated correct, but it is very unlikely. The most likely is the one that I spoke about, 3.5 plus 1.5 equals 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I come back to my first proposition. If Mr. Hamill is right, if he was honorable and honest and careful and calculating from the craters, the shells originated apparently due west, making all allowances for wind and everything else even on your own analysis, there's no way those shells could have come from the Vlasic feature which is 45 degrees away.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you accept, in general, for rounds being fired, since you raised the question of statistics -- Your Honour, just give me a minute. Would you accept and I'm sorry not to be able to use the proper terminology of statisticians, I'll have to use layman's talk, would you accept that artillery rounds will fall as to 68 per cent of them within 2.5 per cent either way of their target and that 95 per cent of them will fall within 5 per cent either way of their target? Do you accept those statistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you repeat it slowly? I didn't get all the figures. I suppose these are common artillery facts, but I should like, before I say yes or no, I'd like to know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course I'll repeat them in a tabular form and I'd note one last figure as well. 68 per cent within 2.5 degrees either way, 95 per cent within 5 degrees either way, and 99.5 per cent within 7.5 degrees either way.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think these are the normal scattering characteristics of these weapons, that is what it is. We know those well-known artillery scattering intervals, that is well-known, that is correct. I don't know exactly these scattering figures. Mr. Hamill will know these figures by heart but, yes, that is correct. However, if you wish, I do have firing tables and I can look at them and then I can give you an accurate answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, can I suggest -- well, we will be having a break at some stage and it may be, although we shouldn't impose on you over a break, but that would be a useful use of your time. But finally, may I suggest to you that however strong the wind may be, the maximum deviation that the wind is going to cause for this type of shell would be about 3 degrees and no more.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what do you say is the maximum deviation a wind could achieve for a shell of this general magnitude?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: For 122 millimetres, I have tables here, and one knows what the deviation is for a particular wind. If the wind is twice stronger, then it's twice as big; three times, three times. It is -- mostly the linear correlation depends on the strength of the wind. I can give you the figures if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient to deal it during the break. We are going to have a break about this time. Is that a convenient moment, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably as convenient as any, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got much more for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have got quite a lot. I'm confident that I will be able to deal with both witnesses in the course of today, but this is evidence clearly to be taken carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, if you'd like to look at your tables for those points about which you were asked, and then you can refer to them afterwards. Don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over. We'll break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, can you help us with any researches made over the short adjournment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is a sketch and it is not done to scale. The angles are smaller. I enlarged them only to facilitate their understanding. Look here. This is the effect of the wind. This is the crosswind. The projectile will deviate like this. And let's say it had fallen here. In the firing tables, what the artillery people are using is this angle here. For instance, for the crosswind of 10 metres per second, the tables show that this is 20 millimetre. When you translate that into the Russian tables, it's 1.2 degree. But the level of the crater is this. This is the plane. And as you see, this angle does not appear in any firing tables. The artillerymen have no use for it. But I created a computer simulation, and in this case the angle most probably was 3.5 degrees. I assumed that the crosswind at the ground level was near zero and that at 6.000 metres was most probably 16 metre per second, and the computer gave me the result of 3.5 degrees. So one should not confuse that angle with this angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't, of course, seen these workings, but are you still saying that the maximum deviation for reasons of wind at the end of the projectile's path is 3.5 degrees from whatever was intended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not the maximum. Most probable. And I serve that with full responsibility. I can also give you a demonstration. I have a computer. I have a NATO model, MPMM, modified point materiel model.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This assumes a 10-metre-per-second wind, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. The 3.5 degrees was a result for the wind at zero -- at the ground level, because the witnesses testified that there was no wind at the time. But I don't know what the wind was in the higher altitude. So I took just a value from the tables, which means that even though there was no wind at the ground level, that does not mean that it was not there at the higher altitudes, and I just assumed that it increased as you went higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course you're -- and the last point I'm going to ask on this, because we haven't been served with advanced detail of all this. But the last point I'm going to ask on this is as follows. Perhaps you'll look at my spectacles. They'll do. I'm holding something up, Dr. Jankovic. It's the easiest way of dealing with something. Dr. Jankovic, could you look at me, please. If this is a projectile going through the air and there's a wind coming from your direction, it's not necessarily going to be turned around as if by the front wheel of a car; the wind is going to move the thing across laterally, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There are two factors to be considered. It's pretty difficult. First, we assume here the so-called Didion principle; that is, the area with this -- with the wind, there is -- and as the space moves, the projectile moves with it. But the projectile changes its speed, its velocity. It slows down going up and then again increases going down. The wind will have the most effect where the velocity is at its lowest, and the effect of the wind is going to be the highest there. And whether it spins, gyrates, it's more of a scientific point. I can discuss it with you here, but I don't think that we should go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very quick point on the short diagram. I'm going to ask you to look at -- I've only got one point at the moment -- on the ELMO. This is a diagram dealing with statistics built entirely on the observations you have made this morning, and therefore taking them, which we don't accept, but taking them on the figures you assert. And if we could have the bottom right-hand corner of the picture in as well. Thank you very much. This is a -- you'd accept, would you not, that if your 5 per cent is accurate, what this shows -- I'm sorry it's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See if we can get it clearer. It's very light at the moment. Well, if it's not going to work, I'll have to have it back and I'll put it to you in verbal form. It's too light. Can I have it back? We can't afford the time, I'm afraid. No, I'll have it back and I'll deal with it. My mistake. I'll take it back. Perhaps we can get it copied, if we can. I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return, please, to your report, and I want to deal with some things quickly. Have you got your report open at page 4, paragraph 6? Mr. Hamill's conclusion, as you know, that the calibre was 122 millimetres, was built on the firing tables available to him at the time, and there's nothing wrong with him making that conclusion if those were the only tables available to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That may be correct, but that is not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since I'm not going to challenge, probably, the firing tables you produce, what it amounts to is: From the firing tables provided to him, he found one calibre shell; you show that there were two others that had the same fuse, and we don't challenge that, all right? Paragraph 7, just as a matter of detail, line 2, Mr. Hamill never said anything about the thing being of Russian origin. The word "Russian" doesn't appear in his evidence, I don't think. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I may have read it in another witness' finding that there were Russian Cyrillic letters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 we don't challenge. Just summarise it because it's helpful and important. It's a little hard to find. You've got three possible projectiles, three possible weapons. In fact, I don't think there's anything else I do need to say on that, but I do need to look at your footnote. "The Prosecution's witnesses are not unanimous on this conclusion." The conclusion that you're referring to here as to the calibre of the shell. "The Zenica investigating judge, who conducted a contemporaneous investigation of the shelling, wrote in his report, and testified, that the calibre of shells used in the shelling was 155 millimetres," and you refer to the Blaskic testimony of the witness Veseljak. I think it's correct, as you will recall, that Veseljak actually first led -- reached the conclusion 155 on a day when he said it was very difficult to do tests, because everything was in the state of crisis, accepted that he was subsequently given reports to suggest that it was 122 but, nevertheless, stuck to his original report because he'd already drafted it as instructed or as commissioned on the first day and stuck to 155. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and 155 was not mentioned by Veseljak but rather by the expert who was part of the commission together with Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1019.2 is indeed the other report that was available to Veseljak which was prepared with just a little more time and a little less crisis and, of course, you are in the happy position of being able to read the original or the English version, but in English, it reads, from Husein Hadzimejlic on the 5th of June, and this was an expert opinion on the shelling of Zenica that, "On the 19th of April between 12.00 and 1.00, the centre of the town was shelled." Next sentence, "Carried out by HV Croatian units from a 122-millimetre howitzer from their position in the Puticevo section on the right-hand side of Nova Bila-Travnik road. Information gleaned from pieces of shrapnel and artillery hits that were noticed spread out on the ground. Contact fuse, high explosives, OX-462Z, six shells in total." No doubt, if you're going to refer to Veseljak's opinion, you'd accept that it's fair to take into account, if we are to take into account at all, the contrary opinion prepared a few days later.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed that during the previous trial of Mr. Blaskic. If it was 122 millimetre calibre, it does not have the range, it cannot reach from Puticevo to the centre of Zenica. It cannot reach Zenica from Puticevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come over that as we turn over the page to page five, paragraphs 9 and onwards. I have nothing to say about paragraphs 9 or 10 now that the Russian word has become irrelevant. Paragraph 12, your conclusions, the RGM fuse can be used on each of the projectiles, 122-millimetre howitzer with a range of 15.3 kilometres would, in fact, cover the distance from Puticevo to Zenica. There's a map there if you want to check it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I checked it if -- on the map where -- which I consulted, I did not see Puticevo, so I cannot say what the distance is between Puticevo and Zenica. My understanding is that it was out of range, but somebody has to determine exactly where this Puticevo is so that we can measure the exact distance from the centre of Zenica, and from the map which I used, it was 16 kilometres from this Puticevo to the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, you've just told us that in Blaskic, you told the Court that it was out of range and now you tell us you've never measured the distance. How can that be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not measure the distance on the ground, I measured it on the map. And on the map, I showed 16 kilometres. And -- but someone has to know the exact distance. I don't know the exact distance. I only showed it on the map. From what I was able to determine by reading the map, it was 16 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know, of course, Mr. Hamill, unlike you, visited the area, and I'm going to come to this right at the end and, indeed, found an area in Puticevo suitable for firing in the direction of Zenica. Now, if he measured it and found it could be within range, you've got no reason to challenge him on that, have you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no reason, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because Puticevo is an area probably itself 2 kilometres in extent. If we stay with paragraph 12, the position, I think, is this, that the Croats at that time had 122-millimetre howitzers. What weapons of either of these two gauges did they have, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So far as I know, the Croats in Central Bosnia had the 152-millimetre calibres. I'm not aware of them having the other calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So of course the 152-millimetre howitzer would have no trouble reaching Zenica from Puticevo. It would be well within range.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the three weapons, that's looking at it from the Croat's point of view, they had two weapons, assuming Mr. Hamill is right, the 122 and the 152, which could easily have reached Zenica from Puticevo. If we now look at the Serb side, and you may want to have another look at the map which, I'm so sorry, is inconveniencing the interpreters, and perhaps I'll take it down after this exercise and have it moved, if you look due west from Zenica, and think of the three weapons that could have carried this fuse and asked yourself the question: Could the Serbs have fired from due west? The answer comes as follows: 122 millimetre would have had insufficient range, couldn't have done it. Likewise, the 130 millimetre one which we've just been referring to at 27.5 kilometres would have had range from the left of that red line, that red front line would have had range to reach Zenica. The third one, the 152 millimetre one which has a range of only 24.4 kilometres would not reach; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And even so, the one with the longest range of 27.5 kilometres would only just be able to reach from Serb-held territory, and the problem there is that out west of Zenica at that point of the map, and we can all see straight left, there's no suitable territory there for firing this type of artillery piece; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn over then please to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we take that down now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Nice, if you'd have regard to the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I will actually have one question about that map so if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. To do that now, may I have leave just to approach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, it's been put to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, it's been put to you that it's a 45 degree angle from Mount Vlasic to the centre of Zenica, but Mount Vlasic, if you take a look at the map, is actually an extremely large area, it's a tabletop mountain that lies to the north of Travnik and covers a very large area in here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not on that mountain, but that is my impression just by observing the map. [In English] I think so. I wasn't there but I think so looking at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Topographically, you can see that the map has a tabletop fairly even surface that stretches over a wide area which is why it's such a commanding, strategically important feature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may -- it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Puticevo is this little feature here that was outlined by Mr. Nice, and I believe Vlasic comes down to this point and comes up to this point at the north --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I believe we're now getting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're now getting to the stage of Mr. Sayers giving evidence. There's no evidence to this effect at all, the evidence about where Vlasic is has all been to the contrary effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we are going to need some further evidence on this particular topic. In any event, the witness really can't give evidence about it but your point is that -- go on about Puticevo, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point is, Your Honour, that Puticevo is here where I'm indicating. The southerly point of Vlasic, the Vlasic plateau is here. Puticevo here, southerly point of the Vlasic plateau here. And if you measure the angle from the southern point of the Vlasic plateau to Zenica, you get a completely different angle at the southern point than you do from the northern point which was using the 45 degree point that Mr. Nice referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's just a matter of cartography, but we're more than happy to produce the one who's familiar with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whether we need that or not, it doesn't matter. That sounds like a matter for argument. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the second question is simply a matter of measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We viewed a map, the Zenica 4 series, yesterday and measured the distance from the Puticevo feature to the centre of Zenica, where the shells fell, and I think you've said that that distance was 16 kilometres. Was that within or outside the range of a D-30J 122-millimetre artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said so. I measured 16 kilometres, and that is out of the 122-millimetre howitzer's range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what is the range of the 122, then, Dr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is really dangerous to answer that question, because there are two standards whereby the range is determined: There is the NATO standard and the Russian standard. Usually one uses the Russian standard because it being a Russian weapon, and its range is about 15 kilometres, 300 metres, perhaps a few metres less. That is according to the Russian standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take the map down now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Jankovic, just help me, please. I asked you before this adjournment whether we could eliminate Vlasic as of relevance because it was too far away. You're now being reminded of what you looked at yesterday at the map and you give a different answer. How? How can that come, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, it all depends on where those weapons are and what is Vlasic. It is known exactly what is the range of weapons. If any of their positions were within that range, then they could have fired; if not, then, naturally, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Equally, when you return to what the position was in May and the conclusions were of shellings coming from an area six kilometres north of Travnik, that was a part of Vlasic well outside any parameters of error on the part of shells for these purposes; it was far too far away, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have to look exactly at where the position is, where are these 24 kilometres -- for 152, that's 24 kilometres -- and if so, if it's possible, then it's possible; if it's not possible, then it's not possible. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, when I explain to you that Mr. Hamill, who had about there, found the area and measured it and said it was within range, you accepted it. Can you help me, please, with how you then change your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know where the weapon was. If Mr. Hamill says that it was within the range, then it is so. If it was outside that range, then it is not so. I cannot say whether it was within or not, because I do not know where the weapon was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now, then, look, please, at the same exhibit, that is, the general Exhibit D202.1. But may we look at tab 15, which is actually Exhibit D164.1. Sorry, D164/1. First of all, then, if we look at -- sorry. If we look at D164/1, a milinfosum, that's a military information summary, for the 6th of June, a little later, it says this of the location of weapons, so far as the BSA is concerned. Under D -- do you see that? -- it gives there 122- and 155-millimetre howitzers and it gives the reference points, which we can all see, all in the Vlasic feature and all quite close together. And they're all far to the north. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just object to the form of that question, Your Honour, because it's quite clear that this milinfosum refers to artillery dispositions of the BSA in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can help us with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may have to turn up in argument. But can we then turn to the next exhibit in the bundle, which is Z1044, one of the Defence exhibits. I can always make mine available if it would help. It's part of, and I'll just -- I'll hand it all to the usher, but open at the one line I want. It's a milinfosum for the 11th of June, and it's that sheet. Lay it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is again a military information document, and what it says, in relation now to the Croat disposition of forces, we can see, in the Vitez area, under paragraph 11, is that there were 255 Nora howitzers in the Mosunj quarry. Well, do you know this: The Mosunj quarry is not only not on Puticevo; it's a little bit south of Puticevo, but well within range of Zenica. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know anything about it. I do not know. But Nora is 152-millimetre calibre, so this has to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, for the want of time, I'm going to pass over that particular point, although I could deal with it. And can we return, please, now to your report. And we are on to the last page -- no, not the last page -- page 6, where you deal first with crater analysis to ascertain calibre of shells. And I'm not going to deal with that, because what you're saying is it's an inaccurate method, isn't that correct, imprecise method?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate that issue with you. The Court has heard some witnesses who rely on it, but I'm not challenging in substance what you say about its limitations. If we go to paragraph 15, you make some references there to the sort of ground that these craters fell on. Asphalt is a very good surface, would you accept, for what we find on the following page, page 7, at paragraph 17, which is the only analysis of craters done by Mr. Hamill?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know what term I'm supposed to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with this in stages. First of all, your report, it happens, doesn't deal with Mr. Hamill's evidence really at all on the use he made of crater analysis. You don't comment on it at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that your choice or the lawyer's?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was my choice, because my approach is as I've written it down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill made no attempt to gauge the type of shell from the crater; he used the crater only to deal with the direction of incoming fire. You accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do for an approximate determination of the direction. That is what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He did not do it by photographs, as seems to be being implied at some stage in the evidence. As you must know from his evidence, he visited the area, looked at the existing craters, and was able to confirm what they were by reference to photographs taken at the time. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now, please, look at the document that was earlier not visible on the ELMO, and which can be distributed as Exhibit 2822.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I repeat, Doctor, that I'm not a statistician, and my understanding of terms you were referring to is therefore untutored. But I think what you talked about when you spoke of the Gaussian distribution is something we can reduce to understandable terminology with which I hope you will agree. This little diagram is built on your own calculations of a standard 5 per cent deviation, and what it shows is that on the basis of your figures of 5 per cent -- which we don't necessarily accept, but 5 per cent -- 68 per cent of firings would land within 5 per cent either side; 95 per cent would land within 10 degrees of either side; 99.5 per cent would land within 15 degrees of either side; and the remaining half per cent would lie outside that range. Converted into something that the layman can easily understand, would you accept that there is a 1 in 200 chance of an error more than 15 degrees, a 1 in 20 chance of an error more than 10 degrees, a 2 to 1 chance of an error more than 5 degrees, and a 1 to 2 chance of an error less than 5 degrees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Artillerymen, gunmen, they call this one probable deviation, and this area, plus/minus so much, is 50 per cent, which means that 50 per cent is within and 50 per cent without, and that is the most probable value that I used. So when I said that the angle was most probably 5 degrees, it means that the chances -- that the odds are 50 per cent that it will be within these 5 per cent and 50 per cent that it will be without. And then the probability goes more or less as you described it. There is a very low probability that it could be as large as that. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now these probabilities, thank you for that. If we can put that on --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing more. May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So the most probable value here, if we're talking about the maximum, the word that you used then we mean this one here, four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, that distribution of variation is, as it were theoretical, built on your factual assumption about five per cent. Of course, theoretical determinations have to be modulated by real experience of a particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I hand in Exhibit 2260 which I have lightly highlighted, 2260.3, which I have lightly highlighted, to assist the witness and if it can go on the ELMO. I hope the highlighted colours will show up. I don't think they do very satisfactorily but to some degree they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've tried to highlight the shell position landing in yellow and green, but the green shows up, the yellow doesn't very well. The evidence has been, Dr. Jankovic, if you look at the bottom of the two pairs of colours, that there was a yellow and green shell landing in that southern position. Further up the page, there was a yellow one more significantly to the left, and then the green one near the apex of the little triangle that's formed there, and then at the top, and again the yellow one isn't very easy to see, there was two more shells, one yellow one green close together. That's what was found on the ground. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Dealing with the one that's a little further to the left or west, that is the one in the middle, the shortfall of that shell could easily be explained, could it not, by what you were saying about some shells being of different weight in times of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Different weight markings, as we call that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That can easily explain that. But the general extreme close proximity of these shells one to another shows, does it not, that they fall within -- on our statistical diagram, well within the central area of the five per cent error and, frankly, they show a pretty high level of accuracy. You would accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I calculated that and that is a difficult question to answer. The statistical scattering of these shells can mean that they belong to the same -- to one and the same group but it does not have to mean that. That is both answers are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we accept the evidence for the time being, that the order in which the shells landed was as follows: The bottom two first, the middle two next, the top two last. With your knowledge of the army, that is entirely consistent with there being somebody providing information of where shells are landing and that information being reported back to the artillerymen, and then making appropriate adjustments to their firing in order to better reach their targets.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Other explanations are also feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's deal with that in two stages. First of all, what I propose to do which is what Mr. Hamill gave in evidence is one explanation and I'd like it correct and then please tell us what the other explanations are.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: What Mr. Hamill said is correct, either explanations are. I know from the rules of firing of the Yugo army when you fire at a target with a certain area, then the firing direction changes over time, and this could have been the case of firing at a surface target, that is, as Mr. Hamill said. I could agree that there were two weapons which were firing, that one projectile and then they changed the direction, again, they fired one projectile each, then they slightly shifted direction and then again takes turns. So that is another possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If these shots were fired in the way suggested, moving first once and then the second time in a northerly direction, and if the firing then stopped, that would again, as Mr. Hamill has suggested, fit with there being an intended object and with that object having been effectively hit; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, but again, there may be other explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's always possible that everything is entirely at random, but there's no reason to believe that these firings were entirely at random, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.
